# Writing in Markdown {#sec-markdown}

Markdown is plain text with punctuation that describes **structure** rather than
appearance. You identify something as a heading, quotation, citation, or code
expression; the output format decides how that structure should look.

That separation is what allows the same source to become a web page, PDF,
Word document, book chapter, slide deck, or tutorial.

## Source versus appearance

In a word processor, “make this 18-point bold” is a visual instruction. In
Markdown, `## Methods` says “this is a second-level heading.” Quarto can then:

- number it in a PDF;
- put it in an HTML table of contents;
- turn it into a slide boundary;
- include it in navigation; and
- give it an address for cross-referencing.

Semantic structure is both more reusable and more accessible than manual visual
formatting.

## Document metadata

A Quarto document begins with YAML metadata between `---` lines:

```yaml
---
title: "A reproducible analysis"
subtitle: "A synthetic training study"
author: "A. Researcher"
date: today
bibliography: bibliography.bib
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
---
```

The YAML is configuration. It answers questions such as:

- What is the document called?
- Who wrote it?
- Which bibliography should be used?
- Which outputs should be created?
- Which options differ between those outputs?

Indentation defines nesting:

```yaml
format:
  html:             # belongs under format
    toc: true       # belongs under html
  pdf:              # also belongs under format
    number-sections: true
```

If `toc` were aligned with `format`, it would have a different scope.

## Headings create document structure

Use one `#` for a level-one heading, two for level two, and so on:

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
# Introduction

## Background

## Research question

# Methods

## Data

## Analysis
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered structure**

```text
1 Introduction
  1.1 Background
  1.2 Research question
2 Methods
  2.1 Data
  2.2 Analysis
```

The precise numbering and typography come from the output format.
:::
:::

Do not skip from `#` to `###` simply because you prefer the smaller font. That
creates a broken outline for navigation and assistive technology. Change the
*theme* if the visual design needs adjustment (more on this later).

## Section numbering and cross-references {#sec-section-crossrefs}

Turn on numbering for an output:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
```

Give a heading a stable identifier:

```markdown
## Statistical analysis {#sec-statistical-analysis}
```

Refer to it with:

```markdown
The model specification is described in @sec-statistical-analysis.
```

Quarto writes “Section 3.2” or the appropriate number. If the section moves,
the reference updates automatically.

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
## Data preparation {#sec-data-preparation}

Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.

## Statistical analysis

See @sec-data-preparation before fitting the model.
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered idea**

> **3.1 Data preparation**  
> Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.
>
> **3.2 Statistical analysis**  
> See **Section 3.1** before fitting the model.
:::
:::

Stable identifiers are better than writing “see the section above” or manually
typing “Section 3.1”. Use short, descriptive, lowercase labels separated by
hyphens.

Quarto uses the same system for sections, figures, tables, equations, listings,
and exercises:

| Object | Label prefix | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Section | `sec-` | `@sec-methods` |
| Figure | `fig-` | `@fig-change` |
| Table | `tbl-` | `@tbl-summary` |
| Equation | `eq-` | `@eq-change` |
| Listing | `lst-` | `@lst-model` |

## Paragraphs and emphasis

A blank line starts a new paragraph. A single line break in the source normally
continues the same paragraph, allowing you to wrap source text without changing
the rendered prose.

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
This is one paragraph even though the
source wraps across two lines.

This is a new paragraph with *emphasis*,
**strong emphasis**, and `inline code`.
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered**

This is one paragraph even though the
source wraps across two lines.

This is a new paragraph with *emphasis*,
**strong emphasis**, and `inline code`.
:::
:::

Use emphasis to convey meaning, not to simulate headings. Backticks are useful
for filenames, functions, variables, and short commands.

## Lists

Unordered lists use `-`; ordered lists use `1.`. Markdown can number ordered
lists automatically:

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
The analysis will:

- read the source data;
- derive the change score; and
- produce a figure.

The reader should:

1. open the project;
1. render the manuscript;
1. inspect the output.
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered**

The analysis will:

- read the source data;
- derive the change score; and
- produce a figure.

The reader should:

1. open the project;
2. render the manuscript;
3. inspect the output.
:::
:::

Using `1.` for every ordered item makes rearranging source easier. Use explicit
numbers only when the source number itself matters.

## Links, images, and footnotes

```markdown
[Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/)

![A concise description of the image](images/result.png)

This claim needs a qualification.[^qualification]

[^qualification]: The data are synthetic and illustrate workflow only.
```

Good link text tells the reader where the link goes. Avoid “click here”.

Image text inside `![...]` becomes alternative text. Describe the information a
reader needs, not merely the filename or “image of a graph”.

Footnotes are appropriate for supplementary explanation. If information is
central to interpreting the result, keep it in the main text.

## Quotations and block quotes

Prefix quoted paragraphs with `>`:

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
> Reproducibility is a property of a
> workflow, not simply a file format.
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered**

> Reproducibility is a property of a
> workflow, not simply a file format.
:::
:::

For published words, include a citation and page or section locator where
appropriate. Markdown syntax does not remove scholarly attribution
requirements.

## Callouts

Callouts separate warnings, definitions, tips, or assumptions from the main
narrative:

````markdown
::: {.callout-warning}
The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.
:::
````

::: {.callout-warning}
The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.
:::

Common types are `note`, `tip`, `important`, `warning`, and `caution`. A callout
should add meaning, not turn every paragraph into a coloured box.

## Tables written in Markdown

Small, static tables can be written directly:

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
| Format | Best suited to |
|---|---|
| HTML | Browsing and interaction |
| PDF | Fixed-page distribution |
| DOCX | Editorial workflows |
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered**

| Format | Best suited to |
|---|---|
| HTML | Browsing and interaction |
| PDF | Fixed-page distribution |
| DOCX | Editorial workflows |
:::
:::

Use a code-generated table when values come from data. A hand-written Markdown
table is appropriate for stable explanatory content such as option summaries.

## Mathematics and numbered equations

Inline mathematics uses one pair of dollar signs:

```markdown
The individual change is $\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}$.
```

The rendered result is: the individual change is
$\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}$.

A display equation uses `$$`. Add a label inside braces for numbering and
cross-referencing:

```markdown
$$
\bar{\Delta}_g =
\frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i
$$ {#eq-group-change}

Group means are defined in @eq-group-change.
```

$$
\bar{\Delta}_g =
\frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i
$$ {#eq-group-change}

Group means are defined in @eq-group-change.

## Citations and bibliographies {#sec-citations}

Bibliographic records live in `bibliography.bib`. A record has a citation key:

```bibtex
@article{knuth1984,
  author = {Knuth, Donald E.},
  title = {Literate Programming},
  year = {1984}
}
```

Use the key in prose:

::: {.writing-demo}
::: {.demo-source}
**Source**

```markdown
Literate programming was formalised by
@knuth1984.

Reproducibility requires more than
retaining code [@sandve2013].
```
:::

::: {.demo-output}
**Rendered**

Literate programming was formalised by @knuth1984.

Reproducibility requires more than retaining code [@sandve2013].
:::
:::

Quarto formats the citation and builds the reference list. A Citation Style
Language (`.csl`) file can change the style without rewriting citations.

Useful citation patterns include:

```markdown
[@knuth1984]                 # parenthetical
@knuth1984                  # textual author
[@knuth1984, pp. 100–102]   # locator
[@knuth1984; @sandve2013]   # multiple sources
```

The bibliography automates formatting, not source evaluation. Check names,
titles, dates, identifiers, and whether the cited source supports the claim.

Probably the easiest way to get bib keys is from [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/) and the [Better BibTeX extension](https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/) which can export the required format for a `.bib` file automatically.

## A fuller Markdown exercise

In `manuscript.qmd`:

1. Complete the title, subtitle, author, and output options in YAML.
2. Create Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References sections.
3. Add stable `sec-` identifiers to Methods and Results.
4. Refer to Methods from the Results prose.
5. Add a research question, bulleted aims, and the numbered change-score
   equation.
6. Add one citation, one footnote, one link, and one warning callout.
7. Render to HTML and inspect the table of contents, numbering, and references.
8. Render to PDF and identify what changed visually and what remained
   semantically the same.

::: {.checkpoint}
### Checkpoint

The source contains structure rather than manual styling. Headings appear in
navigation, section and equation references update automatically, and citations
are generated from the bibliography.
:::

@sec-computation applies the same source-to-output principle to calculated
values, figures, and tables.
